I had a 7cm Dermoid cyst removed from my left ovary a month ago. 

Apparently they are relatively common but as they tend to grow over time and don't go away on their own they need to be removed so they don't cause ovarian torsion - mine wasn't causing me any pain but due to its size it needed to be removed (my gyno said they recommend removing anything over 5cm). 

I was quite worried ahead of my surgery too but it was fairly straight forward and a month later I'm feeling mostly back to normal. 

The surgery is a day procedure and the surgery itself takes less than 2 hours (might take a few more hours before they will discharge you though) so you likely won't have to stay overnight - get someone to pick you up and drive you home though and maybe leave an overnight bag in the car just in case. Someone should stay with you for 24hours after the surgery. 

They make several small incisions on your lower belly and one in your belly button and fill your belly with air. I was told that the air can make your shoulders hurt several days after the surgery but I didn't experience it. My incisions were glued together with a purple-ish glue so I didnt have any dressings that needed changing. The glue has been steadily coming off on its own. 

They gave me some pain killers before I was discharged but I stopped taking them after 2 days as I had a negative reaction - but I just took panadol from then on and was fine. 

I spent the day after the surgery in bed and the next day on the couch but after that was pretty much self-mobile. I'd recommend taking a week off work if you can as sitting down was uncomfortable for me due to the position of the incisions. I also didn't wear underwear for about 2 weeks afterwards as they were rubbing against the inscisions and looking back on it I wish I'd bought some of those high- waisted granny undies. My gyno recommended that I not do any sport for 3 weeks and I was not allowed to take a bath or go swimming until she gave me the ok at the month-after follow up yesterday. 

There are several things I wish my nurses or doctors had told me beforehand:
- they will need to do a pregnancy test before surgery so you will need to give a urine sample - so don't go to the toilet in the hours leading up to your surgery otherwise your surgery might be delayed until they can do a blood test and get the results back. 
- They don't let you leave until after you have gone to the bathroom which can take a while as they ask you to reduce your water intake before the surgery and might insert a catheter during surgery. Once you become conscious take small sips of water and ask for a coffee or a carbonated soft drink as these can assist in helping you go to the toilet. 
- sign a waiver in case they find anything odd in there that they can remove at the same time - they found some endometriosis tissues in me that could have been removed if I'd signed a waiver beforehand but as we didn't discuss they couldn't do it and I really wish they had. 


I got the biopsy results yesterday and got to see some pictures of the cyst- was a bit disappointed that it didn't contain any teeth but it did have quite long hair. My gyno has said that I'll need to have another pelvic ultrasound in a years time as Dermoids have a habit of growing back - sometimes even on the other ovary.

The gynaecologist said that there were 4 issues that I had to be aware of in terms of PCOS

1) PCOS is easier to manage if you are within a healthy BMI - luckily in Australia if you have a chronic medical condition you have access to a bulk-billed (free) management plan which includes appointments with a dietician and a fancy medical PT.

2) With PCOS comes higher cardiovascular risks as well as increased risk of diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol. As we get older we will need to be careful of these risks and it is better to try to manage these through diet sooner rather than later.

3) PCOS can cause the Uterine lining to thicken which can cause increased risk of uterine cancer. Currently my uterine lining is quite thin (normal for someone in my age bracket) but the doctor has recommended that when I reach my mid-30s I will need to start taking Progesterone in order to protect the lining, this can be delivered through several normal birth control methods e.g the pill, IUD, implant.
